messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 25
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Salesperson
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 76

He remembers the first shell. It landed three blocks from his apartment building, a sound that seemed to come from inside his own skull. He was twenty-two then, working as a junior sales rep for a European logistics firm that had just opened an office in a city that, six months later, would no longer appear on most maps. The morning it started, he had been on a routine client call, discussing container shipping rates. An hour later, the roads were clogged with dust and panic. He walked home past a bakery with its windows blown in, the white flour on the street looking like snow. He didn’t know then that he would spend the next eight weeks in that apartment, hearing the thud of artillery every night.

Now, three years later, he is twenty-five, sitting in a showroom in a quiet German town, trying to sell kitchen appliances to couples who argue about stainless steel finishes. His hands are clammy. The overhead fluorescent lights buzz at a frequency that reminds him of the drones that used to circle above the southern district. He blinks, and for a second the customer’s face is smudged, replaced by the pale, waxy cheek of his neighbor—the one who died of shrapnel while collecting water. He blinks again. The customer is still there, waiting for an answer about the warranty.

He tells his girlfriend he doesn’t want to go to the outdoor market on Saturdays. He says it’s too crowded, too loud. What he doesn’t say is that the sound of a motorcycle backfiring makes him drop to one knee, his heart racing so fast he sees spots. He doesn’t tell her that he scans every rooftop before he steps out of the car, or that he counts the exits in every restaurant before he can take a bite. She notices he flinches when she touches him from behind, and she has stopped surprising him with hugs.

His sales numbers have dropped. His manager says he seems distracted, that he loses his train of thought mid-sentence. He does. He’ll be talking about energy efficiency, and suddenly he is back in the stairwell of his apartment building, the concrete shaking, a child crying from somewhere below. He hears that crying in the showroom sometimes, even when no children are there. He checks his email compulsively, even though he no longer has any contacts in that city. He cannot bring himself to delete the old chat threads. He reads them sometimes, late at night, and he sees the last messages from colleagues who never replied—“Stay safe,” “We’re fine here,” and then nothing.

He has not told his girlfriend what he saw. He has not told her that when he finally got evacuated, he had to step over a body in the stairwell, and he did not stop to look. He has not told her that sometimes, in the shower, he hears the screaming that came from the apartment next door. He tells her instead that he is tired. He is always tired. He sleeps badly, wakes at 3:17 a.m. every night—the exact time the first shell hit, though he never checked a clock—and he stays awake, listening for the silence that means another is coming.

Last week, a customer dropped a metal baking tray on the tile floor. The crash sent him backward into a display of refrigerators. He laughed it off, said he was clumsy. But his hands shook for the rest of the shift.

He still smiles at his girlfriend. He still goes to work. But the war is not over for him. It is not a memory. It is a room he carries inside his chest, and every day, he opens the door just a crack, and peeks in, and closes it again. He is not sure how much longer he can keep the door shut.
